FlashRT-PAI: Fast Kernels Are Not Fast Pipelines
for Physical AI Inference

 

Liang Su David Chen Jason Li Kevin Guo Teresa Lv

AnyDevice AI & Alps Lab

††footnotetext: Preliminary work. Under review by the Machine Learning and Systems (MLSys) Conference. Do not distribute.
Abstract

Vision-language-action (VLA), video-action (VA), and world action models (WAMs) form the backbone of modern physical AI systems, yet their real-time single-batch inference remains a defining bottleneck. Latency is dominated not by individual kernel computation, but by system-level overhead: thousands of short kernel launches, intermediate data movement across operator boundaries, and redundant recomputation across consecutive decisions. General-purpose graph compilers cannot address these costs, as they optimize individual calls in isolation and lack visibility into cross-call state semantics and global pipeline structure.

We present FLASHRT-PAI, a low-latency inference engine built around model-hardware pipeline co-design rather than isolated kernel optimization. FLASHRT-PAI combines three core mechanisms: deep kernel fusion with launch overlap eliminates inter-operator boundaries and launch gaps; an execution contract formalizes the pipeline’s stage DAG, update rates, and named buffers to enable cross-decision state reuse and selective refresh; and execution-state capsules enable fast snapshot, restore, and fork of persistent pipeline state. The system also supports drop-in acceleration of unmodified PyTorch models via parity- and latency-gated kernel replacement.

Evaluation covers six policies on RTX 5090 and four on Jetson AGX Thor. At matched 16-bit precision, FLASHRT-PAI is 1.3–3.7×\times faster than official compiled paths. Combining pipeline co-design with reduced precision delivers 3.38–12.66×\times speedup over official eager implementations. In LIBERO-10, four-bit π0.5\pi_{0.5} achieves 94.04% success on Thor and 93.32% on RTX 5090, compared with 92.4% for the measured official FP16 reference. FLASHRT-PAI is open source, distributed via Hugging Face Kernel Hub, and its opt-in π0.5\pi_{0.5} kernels have been adopted into the LeRobot framework.

1 Introduction

Physical AI places learned policies in robot control loops: VLAs map images and instructions to actions Physical Intelligence et al. (2025); NVIDIA et al. (2025), VAs generate video and actions autoregressively Li et al. (2026a), and WAMs jointly denoise future video and actions Black Forest Labs (2026); NVIDIA et al. (2026); Bi et al. (2026). Each call returns an action chunk; its inference budget depends on the host’s observation and action-update schedule. We study this inference component on edge and workstation GPUs, with task-level checks in LIBERO simulation.

Growing policies such as π0.7\pi_{0.7} and FLUX 3 Action have 5–7B parameters Physical Intelligence et al. (2026); Black Forest Labs (2026). On Thor, official π0.5\pi_{0.5} takes 222.64 ms eager and 129.17 ms compiled; FLUX 3 Action takes 1.35 s on RTX 5090 (Table 3). Reducing latency must also preserve action fidelity, since numerical drift can change robot behavior.

Closing this gap takes more than faster individual kernels. We present FlashRT-PAI, an inference engine for low-latency physical AI, guided by a simple principle: fast kernels are necessary but not sufficient Dehghani et al. (2021). For each model–hardware pipeline, FlashRT-PAI decides what can be fused, overlapped, or reused across decisions; an execution contract makes those choices executable. Four limitations motivate these choices.

First, small kernels repeatedly materialize intermediates; deep kernel fusion removes selected boundaries. At batch size one, separate normalization, residual, activation, and quantization kernels between general matrix multiplications (GEMMs) can write values that the next kernel immediately reads. TensorRT NVIDIA (2026h), torch.compile Ansel et al. (2024), and TVM Chen et al. (2018) already fuse common patterns, but some boundaries depend on deployment-specific facts, such as a validated quantization scale and the next GEMM’s input layout. FlashRT-PAI uses these facts to hand-write the producer–consumer path, folding quantization into the producer where precision and hardware permit. In π0.5\pi_{0.5} on Thor, its FP8 decoder layer uses 12 kernels versus 20 for torch.compile+FP8 (§3.2).

Second, remaining kernel dependencies need not serialize all work; launch overlap hides part of their cost. A successor can load weights before it needs its predecessor’s output, but an ordinary graph dependency waits for the predecessor to finish. At eligible boundaries, FlashRT-PAI marks where the successor may start and where it must wait, then applies CUDA’s Programmatic Dependent Launch (PDL) NVIDIA (2026b). PDL is CUDA’s mechanism; FlashRT-PAI supplies the safe kernel points and pipeline order. On top of the already fused π0.5\pi_{0.5} NVFP4 path, it further shortens each decoder layer on Thor (§3.3).

Third, values needed by later decisions are often recomputed; frozen execution state keeps them valid and reusable. In the official π0.5\pi_{0.5} implementation, step-dependent conditioning is rebuilt on every call; LingBot-VA similarly recomputes cross-attention keys and values derived from an unchanged instruction. CUDA Graph replay gives stable addresses but not the application’s rules for when such values become stale. FlashRT-PAI names its fixed and persistent buffers, and records each one’s owner and refresh rule in the execution contract. It can replay captured stages without per-kernel host dispatch and reuse prompt- or step-dependent values across decisions. These named buffers also form an execution-state capsule that can be copied to snapshot, restore, or fork a session (§3.4).

Fourth, optimized kernels are hard to adopt; checked replacements let an existing host use them selectively. Fast TensorRT deployments for policies such as π0.5\pi_{0.5} and GR00T require model-specific integration NVIDIA (2026f); NVIDIA (2026e), and an existing PyTorch host needs a way to check a replacement before using it. FlashRT-PAI packages each replaceable region with a PyTorch reference and its kernels; the host keeps its own path unless the replacement matches the reference and lowers end-to-end latency (§5). FlashRT-PAI kernels are distributed through the Hugging Face Kernel Hub, and LeRobot adopted an opt-in π0.5\pi_{0.5} kernel integration LeRobot contributors (2026).

We evaluate FlashRT-PAI on a Jetson AGX Thor for robot-side inference and an RTX 5090 for workstation inference. Latency and numerical fidelity use fixed or recorded inputs offline; closed-loop task success is evaluated for π0.5\pi_{0.5} and LingBot-VA in LIBERO simulation. We compare official implementations, torch.compile, and available TensorRT deployments (§4), and report public adoption (§6).

1.1 Contributions

This paper makes three contributions:

  • •

    An inference engine built around model–hardware pipeline co-design. We present FlashRT-PAI, an inference engine that bridges policy models and production deployment through joint choices of GEMM tiling, precision, producer–consumer layouts, fusion, and launch overlap. Rather than stopping at isolated operator tuning, the design also accounts for stage boundaries, input-update cadence, and state reuse. Its kernels support checked integration into existing PyTorch hosts while retaining their control loop and fallback path (§3, §5).

  • •

    Three complementary mechanisms for small-batch inference. Deep kernel fusion removes selected inter-operator memory round-trips, and launch overlap reduces waiting at the boundaries that remain. The execution contract records stage dependencies, input-update methods, and named buffers for cross-decision reuse and selective refresh. Execution-state capsules snapshot, restore, and fork declared continuation state through device-local memory copies. In controlled π0.5\pi_{0.5}/Thor runs, reuse reduces decision latency from 37.05 to 21.61 ms; restoring context and generating the next action takes 9.73 ms instead of 21.48 ms for rebuilding it. Reused and restored actions are bit-exact (§3.4, §4.4).

  • •

    Multi-policy evaluation and open-source impact. Across six policies on RTX 5090 and four on Thor, evaluated paths are 3.38–12.66×\times faster than official eager implementations and 1.3–3.7×\times faster than official compiled paths at matched 16-bit precision. Paired LIBERO task checks cover π0.5\pi_{0.5} and LingBot-VA. FlashRT-PAI is open source, with kernels distributed through the Hugging Face Kernel Hub, opt-in π0.5\pi_{0.5} integration adopted in LeRobot, and public developer and vendor acknowledgments (§4–§6).

2 Background and Motivation

2.1 Three Classes of Policy Calls

Figure 1 illustrates one decision cycle for each policy class. In π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Figure 1a), a 27-layer SigLIP encoder embeds each camera view, an 18-layer PaliGemma language model reads the image and prompt tokens (a prefix of about 500 to 800 tokens) and writes its key/value cache, and an 18-layer action expert attends to that cache while integrating ten flow-matching steps over a chunk of ten action tokens Black et al. (2024); Physical Intelligence et al. (2025); Lipman et al. (2022). GR00T N1.7 has the same overall structure NVIDIA et al. (2025). A VA generates video and actions autoregressively, one chunk at a time. In LingBot-VA (Figure 1b), a text encoder reads the instruction once per prompt, a VAE encodes the observed frames, and the backbone denoises the video and action tokens of the next chunk while attending to a key/value cache over earlier chunks; the cache persists from one decision to the next and grows up to a fixed window Li et al. (2026a). A WAM also starts from a video generation model. In FLUX 3 Action (Figure 1c), a frozen Qwen3-VL-4B encodes the instruction, a frozen video VAE encodes the camera frames, and a 7B diffusion transformer denoises future frames together with a chunk of 32 actions Black Forest Labs (2026). Cosmos and Motus follow the same pattern with other backbones NVIDIA et al. (2026); Bi et al. (2026).

All the policy calls share three structural properties:

  1. 1.

    Parts of the call change at different rates: the instruction once per task, the observation once per decision, and the denoising loop several times within each decision.

  2. 2.

    A deployment fixes the number of views, context-length bucket, action horizon, and denoising-step count. These constraints allow fixed-shape stages to be prepared once and replayed.

  3. 3.

    Shapes vary widely within one call. The π0.5\pi_{0.5} action expert processes ten rows per step, whereas VA and WAM backbones process thousands of video and action tokens. These workloads need different GEMM tiling and fusion choices; a VA also carries history state across decisions.

Fixed shapes make replay possible, but they do not by themselves determine the fastest execution path. For these policies, action shapes, the formats exchanged between adjacent kernels, and the lifetime of prepared values guide the design choices below.

2.2 Kernel Boundaries and Cross-Decision Reuse

More capable models alone do not solve physical AI deployment. On both edge devices and workstation GPUs, policy calls remain small-batch and latency-sensitive. Three costs recur at batch size one: intermediate traffic between kernels, waiting at the boundaries that remain, and recomputation of unchanged values across calls. Table 1 profiles intermediate-kernel costs in one complete π0.5\pi_{0.5} decision of the official OpenPI PyTorch eager implementation on Jetson AGX Thor; Figure 3 separately tests launch overlap. Within-call timing cannot show whether a value needed by the next decision was retained or recomputed.

Observation 1: materialized intermediates cost time and traffic. The kernel trace records 70.10 ms in non-matrix kernels between GEMMs, about 31.49% of the unprofiled decision latency in this estimate. They normalize, add a residual, transform a layout, or convert precision. Each separate kernel must start and move its intermediate through memory. Folding eligible operations into neighboring kernels reduces launches and intermediate memory traffic. Figure 3 shows that the problem remains after compilation: with torch.compile and FP8, one action-expert layer still runs 20 kernels. Whether a boundary can be removed depends on the producer’s output and its consumer’s precision and layout (§3.2).

Observation 2: a remaining dependency need not serialize all work. Estimated gaps account for 22.52% of an eager decision (Table 1), and fewer kernels leave fewer gaps (§3.2). Some boundaries must remain, however. At each of them, a plain dependency makes the next kernel wait for its predecessor to end before it starts any work, even setup or weight loading that does not need the predecessor’s output. The bottom pair in Figure 3 shows that such independent work can start early while the dependency is still respected (§3.3).

Observation 3: results needed later can be lost at a call boundary. Figure 1 shows that an unchanged instruction can supply many decisions. Yet a call-scoped path may recompute the embeddings, tables, or K/V derived from it on every call, or recycle an intermediate buffer as soon as its last consumer in that call finishes. In the official π0.5\pi_{0.5} implementation, for example, the time conditioning of each denoising step depends only on the step index, yet it is recomputed at every step of every call. Keeping such values cuts a decision from 37.05 to 21.61 ms (§4.4). Discarding such values repeats work; retaining them without a refresh rule risks using stale data after the instruction or frame changes. The missing information is how long each value remains valid and who may overwrite it (§3.4).

These opportunities require scale, shape, and layout for fusion; safe trigger and wait points for overlap; and update rates, validity rules, and owners for reuse (§3.2–§3.4).

3 Design of FlashRT-PAI

FlashRT-PAI chooses stage boundaries, update rates, shapes, layouts, precision, and capture granularity together. Hand-written kernels implement fusion and launch overlap; an execution contract then records the completed stage DAG and buffer rules for replay and capsules. The FlashRT-PAI engine owns the captured graphs and fixed-address buffers. A session manager uses the exported contract to select stage replays when the application reports changed inputs, and copies declared state for capsules.

3.1 Architecture and Model Integration

Figure 2 maps a loaded checkpoint into stages with declared inputs, outputs, shapes, buffer roles, and update rates. Instruction-dependent work runs at prompt setup; vision, prefix, and action work run per decision. Setup selects kernels and precision, calibrates scales, checks fidelity, prepares slower-changing values, and chooses launch boundaries. It captures the full decision or split context/action stages, then exports the contract.

At decision time, the robot loop fills swap windows with observations and noise; the session manager replays the selected captured stages over fixed-address buffers; and the host reads the action chunk. Declared state regions can be copied as capsules. Integration into an existing host is described in §5.

Across models, the reusable components are the buffer roles, contract and kernel interfaces, and qualification procedure. Stage decomposition, precision, layouts, and trigger/wait placement are designed and validated per model–hardware pipeline; the contract records those choices after design.

3.2 Deep Kernel Fusion

FlashRT-PAI fuses memory-bound work around compute-heavy kernels: examples include residual addition with normalization and output quantization, RoPE with QKV split and cache write, and patch embedding with layout conversion. Compute-heavy GEMMs and attention keep their specialized implementations. We select a fused boundary when a supported fixed shape and layout let the producer emit the consumer’s required format, all consumers remain valid, and the complete path passes fidelity and latency checks. Other boundaries remain separate.

Let the action shape determine the GEMM tile. The π0.5\pi_{0.5} action expert has ten activation rows, while the stock NVFP4 GEMM tile reserves space for 128. For selected decoder projections, FlashRT-PAI swaps the operand roles so that the large tile dimension carries weights and the short dimension carries the ten action rows. The output store also matches the next kernel’s input layout, avoiding a separate transpose. The deployment shape therefore determines both the GEMM tile and the producer–consumer interface (Appendix A.3).

Choose fusion and the consumer’s layout together. For an encoder FFN, FlashRT-PAI packs gate/up weights together so the GEMM can apply the gated activation and produce packed four-bit values directly. The first fused version wrote a full-width result and doubled the next GEMM’s weight traffic, making the feed-forward chain slower. A compact, half-width output preserved the consumer’s original shape and made the chain faster. It also quantized the intermediate once rather than twice. The useful optimization is the complete producer–consumer path: fewer launches help only when the output format also suits the next kernel. Appendix A.3 gives the layout details.

Figure 3 traces a complete π0.5\pi_{0.5} action-expert decoder layer on Jetson AGX Thor. At FP8 GEMM precision, FlashRT-PAI reduces the layer from 20 kernels in the PyTorch torch.compile path to 12. It fuses the small operations around the FFN’s two GEMMs: residual addition, normalization, and input quantization share one kernel, while GeGLU and output quantization share another (§4.3). The NVFP4 path also folds GeGLU into a GEMM epilogue, leaving 11 kernels per layer.

At the fused quantization boundaries in Figure 3, the producer emits the GEMM input and its scale without a separate activation read/write pass. This requires a supported precision, shape, and layout; π0.5\pi_{0.5} still has an attention-output path with separate quantization. Selected low-bit paths use activation-aware weight scaling Lin et al. (2024). Scales are calibrated before capture, cached by checkpoint and sequence length, and checked against model-level fidelity results (§4.5).

3.3 Launch Overlap

Fusion leaves some producer–consumer boundaries intact. Overlap requires input-independent successor work, a safe wait before dependent reads, and a measured gain despite resource contention. At eligible pairs, FlashRT-PAI uses CUDA’s programmatic dependent launch (PDL) to start a successor GEMM’s weight loading before its activation is ready, then waits before reading that activation. The pipeline selects the pair, and the kernels mark safe trigger and wait points that an ordinary graph dependency does not expose NVIDIA (2026b). PDL permits overlapping execution but does not guarantee it; the successor still waits before it reads the predecessor’s output. In the bottom two rows of Figure 3, enabling PDL at the FFN and adjacent O/QKV boundaries shortens the already fused 11-kernel NVFP4 layer from 62.1 to 52.1 μ\mus with the same kernels and precision. CUDA supplies PDL; our design chooses and validates the model-specific trigger and wait points. Appendix A.4 gives three cases, including boundaries where more overlap does not help.

3.4 Execution Interface and Reusable State

The execution contract exposes a completed pipeline through a shared execution interface. Reuse is valid only while the inputs that produced a retained value are unchanged. The interface records stage order, supported shapes, and named buffers with owners, sizes, and update methods. The engine checks stage references and selects a captured replay for the requested shape. Appendix A.1 gives the execution rules, interface fields, and a worked π0.5\pi_{0.5} plan. Static buffers hold prepared values; swap windows hold replaceable inputs and outputs at fixed addresses; state regions retain mutable state between stages or decisions. The engine allocates these buffers once and captures selected stages as CUDA Graphs keyed by shape.

The interface records stage order, input-update methods, and the buffer regions needed for continuation. In π0.5\pi_{0.5}, instruction embeddings can be reused while the instruction is unchanged, whereas a new observation requires rebuilding image-conditioned K/V. If another session overwrites the working buffers, restoring the saved regions lets the original session continue without rebuilding its completed context.

Within a decision. Figure 4 (a) shows the split π0.5\pi_{0.5} plan. The host fills image and noise buffers; context encodes the image and prompt into K/V; action reads that K/V throughout its denoising steps and transforms the noise buffer into the action chunk. Shared named buffers let successive captured stages consume results directly. The session manager orders stage replays according to the contract; captured stages use fixed addresses without replay-time allocation or host-dependent choices. The full-call plan and the split plan return identical actions for identical inputs and noise.

Across decisions. Figure 4 (b) carries prepared values into the next call. The normal π0.5\pi_{0.5} inference path uploads the supplied images and reruns vision and context on every call; it reuses unchanged instruction embeddings and fixed step-conditioning tables. Even the encoder’s text-token K/V depends on the image and is rebuilt. Prompt and robot-state updates enter through the model’s supported input methods. A host driving context and action separately must refresh context for the current inputs before generating the next action.

At a stage boundary, snapshot copies declared restorable regions into an execution-state capsule; restore copies them back, and fork copies them into another session. The export lists region names, offsets, and lengths; loading checks the schema and plan fingerprint, and resumption must respect the model’s chunk boundaries. For π0.5\pi_{0.5}, the capsule holds the context K/V, the prompt embedding, and the decoder position table (14 MB). For LingBot-VA, it also holds the history K/V, the VAE cache, and the random-number state (1.4 GB). After another session overwrites the working buffers, restoring the capsule reproduces the next actions bit for bit, without recapture and without rebuilding the history (§4.4). Capsules remain process-local and plan-specific because captured graphs contain device addresses; they support compatible sessions within a process. Integration defines the complete continuation state and valid resumption points; the session manager copies the declared regions.

4 Evaluation

4.1 Setup

GPUs. We evaluate a Jetson AGX Thor (SM110, 128 GB unified memory, MAXN mode) for robot-side inference and an RTX 5090 (SM120, 32 GB, fixed clocks) for workstation inference. Both are Blackwell GPUs supporting FP8 and NVFP4.

Policies. Table 2 lists six policies: two VLAs, one VA, and three WAMs. All six run on RTX 5090; Thor covers π0.5\pi_{0.5}, GR00T N1.7, LingBot-VA, and Cosmos3-Edge-Policy. Checkpoints and official code revisions are listed in the supplementary material.

Baselines. All baselines are official open-source implementations: OpenPI on Thor and the existing LeRobot reference on RTX 5090 for π0.5\pi_{0.5}, Isaac-GR00T for GR00T N1.7, and the official releases of LingBot-VA, FLUX 3 Action, Cosmos, and Motus Physical Intelligence (2025); Hugging Face (2024); NVIDIA (2025); Li et al. (2026a); Black Forest Labs (2026); NVIDIA et al. (2026); Bi et al. (2026), each run eagerly and with its compiled or CUDA Graph path where one runs. Official TensorRT deployments exist for π0.5\pi_{0.5} and GR00T N1.7 on Thor NVIDIA (2026f); NVIDIA (2026d). Corresponding baseline paths were also tested locally under aligned task protocols; published reference values retain their source markers in Table 3.

Protocol. Experiments run offline on fixed or recorded inputs, excluding physical action execution, network transfer, loading, calibration, and capture. These measurements characterize warmed-up inference; control-loop timing depends on the application’s replanning schedule. Comparisons use matching timing boundaries within each model–hardware pipeline; host-specific intervals are described in Appendix A.2. Paired mechanism experiments use identical preprocessed inputs and pinned noise. Warm-up reaches up to 300 calls on Thor to avoid a lower clock state. Table 3 marks published reference values; other latencies are measured locally. Compiled paths follow the available official implementations. Fidelity uses matched noise and the references specified in Table 7. No result uses approximate denoising-step caching such as TeaCache Liu et al. (2024). Appendix A.2 reports the verified sampling and timing details for the controlled experiments.

4.2 Deployment latency

Table 3 compares FlashRT-PAI with the official eager, compiled, and TensorRT paths, with published deployment references marked separately. For π0.5\pi_{0.5}, FlashRT-PAI is 10.95×\times faster than official eager on Thor and 12.66×\times faster on RTX 5090. GR00T N1.7 is 5.36×\times faster on RTX 5090; its 24.39 ms Thor result compares with the published eager reference of approximately 126 ms (about 5.2×\times). For LingBot-VA on Thor, a chunk takes 0.92 s instead of 9.31 s (10.11×\times), and on the RTX 5090 it is 5.72×\times faster. Among the WAMs, FLUX 3 Action and Motus are 4.91×\times and 7.10×\times faster on the RTX 5090, and Cosmos3-Edge-Policy is 3.38×\times faster on Thor and 4.84×\times faster on the RTX 5090. LingBot-VA/RTX 5090 uses FP8 video-step and INT4 weight-only action-step GEMMs, with the same mixed-precision configuration in the latency and fidelity tables. Appendix A.2 specifies the operator precisions. In the Compile column, the official torch.compile paths are 3.3% slower than eager for Cosmos/Thor and 2.2% slower for LingBot-VA/RTX 5090. LingBot-VA uses the official default compiler settings, which leave parts of the pipeline in eager execution.

Published Thor TensorRT deployments report approximately 49 ms for π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 39.9 ms for GR00T N1.7, compared with FlashRT-PAI’s locally measured 20.33 and 24.39 ms, respectively. For π0.5\pi_{0.5}/Thor, the deployment run has a 20.54 ms p95 over 1000 timed calls after 200 warm-ups, versus a 20.33 ms median.

4.3 Deep fusion and launch overlap

Observations 1 and 2 (§2.2) identify intermediate-kernel costs and independent work across dependent kernels. Deep kernel fusion removes boundaries; launch overlap may hide part of the cost at the boundaries that remain. Table 4 reports latency at each precision tier, Table 5 counts kernels per decision, and Figure 3 gives a measured layer trace and an isolated PDL off/on comparison.

Precision tiers. Table 4 compares the official compiled path with FlashRT-PAI at 16, 8, and 4 bits. Already at 16 bits, without lower precision, FlashRT-PAI is 1.3–3.7×\times faster than the official compiled path. This deployment comparison combines specialized kernels, fusion, graph replay, and value reuse (§4.4). The table compares pipeline configurations at each precision; the 4-bit entries match Table 3. Precision, layout, fusion, and launch scheduling are co-designed: changing one can require conversions or a different kernel schedule. We therefore interpret these rows as complete configurations, rather than independent gains to add. The paired PDL and reuse experiments hold the accompanying implementation fixed to measure those changes within a valid pipeline.

Fusion. Table 5 counts the GPU kernels in one decision. The complete FlashRT-PAI pipelines run 59–93% fewer kernels than official eager paths; the reduction includes fusion and removal of repeated work. In the layer trace of Figure 3, the torch.compile+FP8 path takes 193.2 μ\mus per layer (20 kernels), while the FlashRT-PAI FP8 path takes 105.2 μ\mus (12 kernels). Both use FP8 GEMMs; the FlashRT-PAI layer combines fewer intermediate boundaries with specialized GEMM implementations. This comparison measures the co-designed layer. The NVFP4 path takes 62.1 μ\mus with 11 kernels, combining its precision choice with a fused GeGLU epilogue.

Launch overlap. The bottom two rows of Figure 3 isolate PDL on Thor: the same NVFP4 path replays the same 11 kernels with PDL off and then on at the FFN and adjacent O/QKV boundaries. The layer period falls from 62.1 to 52.1 μ\mus, and the FFN window within it falls from 33.92 to 27.30 μ\mus. In an unprofiled measurement of the whole decoder, enabling PDL at these boundaries lowers the median from 10.124 to 9.207 ms, and enabling it at all decoder boundaries lowers it to 9.009 ms. With PDL at all decoder boundaries, the full call falls from 21.960 to 21.044 ms. All paths run the same kernels at the same precision, a 4.2% whole-call gain in the paired PDL experiment (Appendix A.2). On the RTX 5090, PDL shortens one FFN block of the action expert from 14.56 to 12.09 μ\mus. The whole-call gain is smaller because launch overlap changes only eligible action-expert boundaries; it does not shorten the other stages or host work.

4.4 Frozen execution state

Observation 3 (§2.2) showed that values needed by later decisions are often recomputed. Frozen execution state makes these values explicit: the execution contract names their buffers, owners, and refresh rules. This lets FlashRT-PAI retain unchanged values and copy declared state regions into an execution-state capsule at a stage boundary. Table 6 summarizes these two uses.

Reuse across decisions. We run π0.5\pi_{0.5} on Thor with the deployed NVFP4 engine over eight recorded observations of one task. Both paths replay the same captured graphs; the baseline also recomputes the prompt embedding and the time conditioning of every denoising step into the same buffers. Keeping these values reduces the mean decision latency from 37.05 to 21.61 ms, and the actions stay bit for bit the same. The baseline uses the existing preparation code rather than a separately optimized implementation.

Restore after an interruption. Persistent values can remain in place while one session runs uninterrupted. When sessions share captured graphs and fixed working buffers, however, another session may overwrite them. At a stage boundary, snapshot copies the declared state regions into an execution-state capsule; restore copies them back before replay resumes. If each session permanently retains its own working buffers, no restore is needed. Capsules serve suspended sessions or rollout branches that share one working set: a saved branch retains declared state without duplicating the entire workspace. Table 6 reports the state footprint and snapshot, restore, and fork times.

For π0.5\pi_{0.5}, we interrupt a session after its context stage, run another session over the shared buffers, and then resume the original session. Rebuilding its instruction- and image-conditioned state and generating the action takes 21.48 ms. Restoring its 14.40 MB capsule and generating the same action takes 9.73 ms. The saved context computation was completed before the interruption; a fresh image would still require a new context stage.

LingBot-VA carries history across action chunks. After another session overwrites its working buffers, our rebuild baseline re-encodes the saved observations and actions to reconstruct the historical K/V, while skipping the earlier denoising computations. At 16 committed chunks, this reconstruction takes 894.71 ms, whereas restoring the capsule takes 11.29 ms. Both paths must then generate the next action chunk. Including that work, time to the next action is 1809.32 ms after reconstruction and 925.27 ms after restoration, a 1.96×\times speedup. Forking the LingBot-VA state into a new session takes 36.03 ms. Figure 5 shows that K/V reconstruction grows from 79.88 ms after one chunk to 894.71 ms after 16, while restoration remains about 11.2 ms because the current implementation copies a fixed allocated state region. Rerunning all past chunks is more expensive still, reaching 14.4 s at 16 chunks.

4.5 Fidelity and task success

Table 7 reports matched-input, matched-noise action agreement against the official implementation, except for the FP16-frontend references marked d. LingBot-VA/RTX 5090 is evaluated on held-out traces without sample filtering. Its six arm channels are reported here; full-action scores including the gripper appear in Appendix A.2.1. On LIBERO-10, π0.5\pi_{0.5} on FlashRT-PAI with 4-bit precision succeeds in 94.04% of trials on Thor and 93.32% on RTX 509011 1 The RTX 5090 result aggregates 4,666 successes over 5,000 trials using ten seeds., compared with 92.4% for the measured official FP16 reference. LingBot-VA’s evaluated FP8/INT4 path succeeds in 97/100 episodes on RTX 5090, versus 98/100 for official BF16, using matched seeds and initial states across ten LIBERO-10 tasks.

5 Deployment

FlashRT-PAI offers native C++, a Python frontend, and selective PyTorch-host replacement. All use its kernels; captured-stage exports share the execution contract (§3.4). Pipeline ownership determines the optimization scope.

Native engine and frontend. The native engine owns the pipeline, fixed buffers, and captured graphs. The host fills swap windows and reports changed inputs; the session manager schedules replay and capsule copies. C++ avoids per-kernel host dispatch. The Python frontend uses the same kernels and stages for integration and evaluation, with Python orchestration, input preparation, and output conversion.

Existing PyTorch hosts. Each replaceable region has a specification and PyTorch reference. Qualification checks inputs, outputs, state, shapes, and loop count; tensor-dependent host branches prevent capture. After host-side calibration, activation requires reference agreement and lower whole-call latency, otherwise retaining the original path. Kernels ship through the Kernel Hub. Graph-safe stages can use capture(fn, windows) and export replay and capsule interfaces. The host retains its control loop; local edits may remove synchronization or enable capture. Host module boundaries limit fusion, and preprocessing, postprocessing, and tensor creation remain outside capture.

Integration work. Engineers specify stage boundaries, buffer lifetimes, precision/layout interfaces, and kernel variants, then validate the complete policy. Loading, calibration, and graph capture execute the specified setup; they do not automatically discover this design. Shared kernels and contract interfaces reduce repeated implementation, but a new model–hardware pipeline still requires model-specific design and validation.

6 Ecosystem Adoption and Impact

FlashRT-PAI is an open-source inference engine (https://github.com/flashrt-project/FlashRT), with kernels on the Hugging Face Kernel Hub. The October 2026 repository snapshot records 658 GitHub stars and 89 forks, alongside the public integrations in Table 8. Its public uses span robot-model developers, host frameworks, and vendor deployment guides. Beyond NVIDIA GPUs, it supports AMD Instinct and Ascend; an external team extended the AMD backend from MI350X to MI300X. Table 8 lists uses documented publicly as of October 2026; latency figures are reported by the adopters under their respective setups.

MindOn reports 82 to 32 ms mean latency for Mind-1 using FlashRT-PAI MindOn (2026). LeRobot’s separate PR setup reports 89.4 to 46.7 ms for opt-in π0.5\pi_{0.5} on RTX 5090: a bit-exact denoising loop reaches 79.3 ms, followed by FP8 feed-forward kernels from the Kernel Hub LeRobot contributors (2026); Hugging Face (2026). The option is disabled by default with BF16 fallback. Jetson AI Lab credits FlashRT-PAI’s Thor results as motivation for its π0.5\pi_{0.5} TensorRT deployment NVIDIA (2026f), used as our published baseline.

7 Related Work

Graph compilers. TVM, TensorRT, and torch.compile provide fusion, layouts, autotuning, and CUDA Graph replay Chen et al. (2018); NVIDIA (2026h); Ansel et al. (2024); NVIDIA (2024). FlashRT-PAI supplies model–hardware precision/layout interfaces and explicit cross-decision state rules, then records the resulting pipeline in a contract. It complements compiler optimization with the input lifetimes and state-update rules of a deployed policy; compiler-generated regions can use the same interface.

Serving systems and reuse. PagedAttention, SGLang, Prompt Cache, and Hydragen share or reuse text-prefix attention state Kwon et al. (2023); Zheng et al. (2024); Gim et al. (2024); Juravsky et al. (2024). Marconi manages hybrid KV/recurrent prefix reuse; HCache accelerates contextual KV restoration Pan et al. (2025); Gao et al. (2025). FlashRT-PAI applies reuse to instruction, step-conditioning, K/V, VAE, and RNG regions with different update rates in a robot loop, under explicit ownership and valid resumption boundaries.

Kernels and LLM runtimes. CUTLASS and FlashAttention supply GEMM and attention kernels NVIDIA (2026c); Dao (2024); FlashInfer adds customizable, graph-compatible attention Ye et al. (2025), Marlin optimizes FP16×\timesINT4 GEMM Frantar et al. (2024), and TensorRT-LLM integrates optimized kernels and LLM request scheduling NVIDIA (2026g). FlashRT-PAI adds policy-stage update rules and compatible resumption boundaries for instruction, observation, step, and history state; these libraries can implement its stages.

VLA inference systems. Ma et al. (2025b) reduce inference overheads for 30 Hz π0\pi_{0}-class execution. BLURR combines prefix caching, mixed precision, and single-step rollout Ma et al. (2025a). EagleVLA combines a llama.cpp engine with foresight-aligned asynchronous inference on Orin Yang et al. (2026); its engine is a FlashRT-PAI provider PKU SEC Lab (2026). Reflex adds batched visual encoding and graph replay Chen et al. (2026); FlashDrive co-designs a driving VLA’s algorithm and system Li et al. (2026b). Some change model computation; FlashRT-PAI preserves architecture and denoising schedule across VLA, VA, and WAM pipelines. Public integrations with EagleVLA-Edge and acknowledgments from APXInf are listed as adoption evidence in Table 8.

Vendor deployments. NVIDIA supplies π0.5\pi_{0.5} and GR00T TensorRT paths NVIDIA (2026f); NVIDIA (2026e), and reports Cosmos3-Edge-Policy at 15 Hz on Thor with 32 actions per inference NVIDIA (2026a). DreamZero combines two-GPU parallelism, compilation, kernels, quantization, and caching Ye et al. (2026). These deployments and FlashRT-PAI all require model-specific integration; FlashRT-PAI shares contract and kernel interfaces.

Model-side acceleration and scheduling. Token pruning Yang et al. (2025), approximate feature caching Xu et al. (2025); Liu et al. (2024), and fewer-step distillation Prasad et al. (2024); Akbari et al. (2026) reduce policy computation, whereas FlashRT-PAI’s state reuse avoids recomputing values whose inputs are unchanged. Real-time chunking Black et al. (2025) overlaps inference with action execution and is complementary to reducing the inference latency itself.

8 Limitations and Conclusion

Limitations. FlashRT-PAI targets small-batch, fixed-shape inference; new shapes need recapture, and new native integrations require model–hardware pipeline co-design, tuning, calibration, and validation (Appendix A). The current evaluation focuses on warmed-up inference on two Blackwell GPUs, with four policies on Thor, six on RTX 5090, and task success for π0.5\pi_{0.5} and LingBot-VA in LIBERO simulation. Physical-robot behavior and complete sensor-to-actuator deadlines are outside this evaluation. Broader hardware and task coverage, sustained control-loop characterization, and multi-session resource accounting are directions for further evaluation. Capsules resume compatible sessions within one process (§3.4).

Conclusion. Fast kernels are necessary but not sufficient. FlashRT-PAI co-designs their interfaces, launch dependencies, and state lifetimes, recording the result in an execution contract. Across four policies on Thor and six on RTX 5090, evaluated paths are 3.38–12.66×\times faster than official eager paths and 1.3–3.7×\times faster than compiled paths at matched 16-bit precision. FlashRT-PAI has delivered tangible impact across industry and the open-source research community (§6): it is open source, its kernels are distributed through the Hugging Face Kernel Hub, and its opt-in kernels have been adopted in LeRobot.

Looking ahead, we envision FlashRT-PAI as a standard inference engine for physical AI, with pipeline co-design providing a reusable foundation for production deployment.

Appendix A Worked Examples

The worked examples below show the contract and verified measurement details, then the deployment facts behind fusion, launch overlap, and state reuse.

A.1 Worked Execution Contract

The contract is exported through a versioned C interface. It lists captured graphs and their supported shapes, named buffers, restorable byte regions, and an identity fingerprint used to match saved state to its execution plan. The model interface adds inputs with shapes and update methods, plus stages with explicit prerequisites.

Execution rules. A retained value can be reused only while its source inputs are unchanged. Stages consume prerequisite outputs valid for the current inputs. Restored state belongs to a compatible plan and resumes at the declared boundary; a new observation still requires a new context stage. These rules specify correct use of the interface. Listing 1 shows two of its records; names and field types follow the implementation.

Engine checks and input updates. Construction rejects stage references to missing graphs or prerequisites that have not been declared. An input that requires processing must provide its update function. Replay requires a captured variant for the requested shape, and restore checks state-layout and plan compatibility. For example, the GR00T N1.7 Thor frontend rejects a second prompt initialization and requires a new frontend instance for a new prompt.

Caller responsibilities. The normal model call performs its declared input processing and stage sequence. A host driving individual stages must submit current inputs and refresh dependent state before action replay. If it omits an update or reuses context from an older observation, the result can be an action based on outdated inputs. Shape and plan checks do not detect such unreported changes. The interface checks execution compatibility; the host retains responsibility for input freshness and the robot’s control loop.

Worked plan. In the split π0.5\pi_{0.5} plan below, the engine owns the fixed allocations and replay handles; the application supplies input updates, and the session manager orders stages and capsule copies.

Preparation writes instruction embeddings and fixed-step conditioning. Context reads images and the prepared prompt and writes K/V. Action depends on context, reads that K/V and the noise window, and produces the action chunk. A fresh observation therefore invalidates context, even when the instruction is unchanged. Each replay plan is selected by its supported shape; changing a shape requires preparation and capture before replay.

At the post-context boundary, the measured capsule contains context K/V, instruction embeddings, and the decoder position table, totaling 14.40 MB. The exported region list gives names, offsets, and lengths; schema and plan fingerprint checks restrict restore to a compatible session. Weights and fixed step tables remain resident and are not copied in this experiment. Restoring this state permits continuation from the completed context; a new image refreshes the context stage. The application supplies the input-change events that determine when retained values are refreshed.

A.2 Measurement Details and Short-Run Distributions

Timing boundaries are specific to each host. The deployed π0.5\pi_{0.5}/Thor infer interval includes image upload, model execution, action transfer, and decoding, excluding prompt setup. The 8.23 ms π0.5\pi_{0.5}/RTX 5090 entry measures captured GPU replay. Cosmos/Thor measures in-process CPU observation to CPU action. GR00T/RTX 5090 measures GPU infer(aux), including fresh vision features and the complete DiT. LingBot-VA/Thor reports the mean over saturated chunks 43–47; its RTX 5090 measurement covers history update and prediction, excluding reset, network transfer, and text encoding. Cosmos/RTX 5090 includes preprocessing, VAE and text processing, denoising, and action formatting in both paths. Published reference ratios retain their original source protocols; they are distinct from the paired PDL and reuse experiments.

The controlled π0.5\pi_{0.5}/Thor state experiment uses engine source e4bd927, PyTorch 2.14.0+cu130, and CUDA 13.0 in a separate host environment from the deployment image. Reuse averages 12 alternating pairs over eight recorded observations; both sides replay identical graphs and differ only in recomputing prompt embeddings and step conditioning. Resume, snapshot, and restore-only statistics use 64 paired trials. Every restored continuation and reuse comparison is bit-exact. The PDL experiment uses the same engine source and kernel inventory, 30 warm-ups and 200 interleaved CUDA-event decoder samples per mode; synchronized whole-call medians span eight recorded observations, with 40 bit-exact gates.

The deployment run uses 200 warm-ups; the controlled state and PDL results report paired changes under the stated configuration. Their 21.61 ms reuse and 21.960 ms PDL-off intervals were collected in the controlled host environment; the 20.33 ms deployment interval comes from the deployment image. The distributions summarize the stated warmed-up runs. Sampling counts and compiler settings are recorded per configuration: Cosmos/Thor uses default torch.compile settings and 60 timed calls per deployment path, with p90 of 1227.45, 1267.09, and 363.86 ms for eager, compile, and mixed 4-bit respectively. Table 4 compares configurations collected across precision tiers and measurement sessions; controlled mechanism changes are measured by the paired PDL and reuse experiments. Capsule results measure state-copy and continuation operations over shared working buffers.

Fidelity samples. π0.5\pi_{0.5} uses eight observations on Thor and 24 real LIBERO frames on RTX 5090; the latter has 16 separate calibration frames. GR00T/Thor uses one single-view observation. The RTX 5090 GR00T result is one two-view LIBERO observation at four denoising steps, compared with the FP16 frontend; its 0.999985 cosine matches the workload of the 7.67 ms latency entry. Cosmos uses 114 requests (38 observations, three noise seeds) on Thor and 60 requests (12 observations, five seeds) on RTX 5090. Motus uses four RoboTwin2 input bundles (Appendix A.2.2). LingBot-VA/RTX 5090 scores 717 chunks from 40 traces held out from calibration, against the official FP32 reference with TF32 disabled. Arm and full-action results are reported below. The evaluated mixed-precision configuration uses FP8 for the video backbone’s cross-attention query/output, self-attention QKV, and FFN output projections, and INT4 weight-only GEMMs for action steps; attention operations and history updates retain their higher-precision paths. It retains 20 video and 50 action denoising steps. This configuration is timed at 455.70 ms and is used for both the filtered diagnostic and the unfiltered results below. For π0.5\pi_{0.5}, LIBERO success rates compare the measured official FP16 reference with the 4-bit FlashRT-PAI rollouts. LingBot-VA uses its official BF16 reference and the FP8/INT4 configuration described above. Its paired evaluation runs tasks 0–9 and episodes 0–9 with the same seeds and initial states: 98/100 successes for the reference and 97/100 for FlashRT-PAI.

Validation represented in the tables. Table 7 reports returned-action comparisons for all six policies, and closed-loop success rates for π0.5\pi_{0.5} and LingBot-VA. The accompanying records cover the following inputs and evaluation settings.

A.2.1 LingBot-VA: unfiltered action agreement

Table 12 reports all recorded chunks, including numerically sensitive ones. Each chunk contains 16 actions with six arm channels and a binary gripper command. We report arm motion separately from the complete action because a change in gripper-switch timing can strongly affect the full-action cosine.

As a diagnostic, 670 chunks have stable arm outputs across numerical configurations of the official reference (relative-L2L_{2} threshold 0.1). This selection uses no FlashRT-PAI outputs. On that subset, arm global/worst cosine is .999691/.985367 for BF16 and .999188/.964353 for the mixed path. The main table uses the unfiltered arm scores.

A.2.2 Motus: four-input action and video agreement

The Stage3 Motus deployment is checked on four RoboTwin2 input bundles using the same ten-step FP4 configuration as the 167.08 ms result, without TeaCache. Each bundle supplies its first frame for calibration. Comparisons use the saved upstream actions and decoded video; Table 13 reports the per-input cosines, summarized over ten graph replays. The main fidelity table reports the range across the four action cosines, rather than treating replays of one input as additional samples.

A.3 Deep Kernel Fusion Examples

Calibrated producer–consumer quantization.

An FP8 GEMM needs an FP8 input and a scale. In a dynamic path, separate kernels may first find the activation maximum and then convert the activation before the GEMM. For the π0.5\pi_{0.5} encoder FFN, FlashRT-PAI measures an acceptable scale on representative task inputs before capture. The preceding normalization kernel then emits FP8 directly at that scale, and its single FFN consumer reads those same bytes. The producer and consumer must be selected as a pair: an FP8 output handed to a BF16 entry is an error, not a useful fallback. Attention-output conversion is one boundary that still uses a separate kernel.

The ten-row action shape.

The π0.5\pi_{0.5} action expert always presents ten rows, but the stock NVFP4 GEMM tile reserves space for 128 activation rows. Its out-of-bounds rows still cost memory-system work. For selected decoder projections, FlashRT-PAI swaps the GEMM operands: the large tile carries weights, the ten activation rows use the short dimension, and a column-major store has exactly the bytes the next kernel expects as row-major output. No transpose kernel is needed. The fixed row count is guarded in the implementation. The fixed deployment shape makes this tile choice valid throughout replay.

Phase fusion across layers.

After an FFN down-projection, the policy must update a residual, normalize for the next layer, and convert its input for the next GEMM. If those steps run as separate kernels, each boundary adds a launch and moves an intermediate through memory. FlashRT-PAI’s practical phase kernel combines the gated residual, next-layer adaptive normalization, and FP8 conversion. The known layer and denoising-step order tells it which next-layer style and scale to read. Figure 3 counts 20 kernels and 193.2 μ\mus per layer on the compiler path versus 12 kernels and 105.2 μ\mus on the composed FlashRT-PAI path, measuring the combined pipeline changes at layer granularity.

QKV split, RoPE, and cache write.

After the π0.5\pi_{0.5} QKV projection, a conventional sequence can split the combined output, rotate query and key positions, and write the key/value cache in separate passes. FlashRT-PAI uses one kernel to do all three while those values are already being visited. The pipeline fixes the head geometry and the K/V cache layout; a device-side valid-prefix position tells the kernel where to append K/V even when prompts are padded to a common capture shape. The cache layout and position rule make the combined write valid throughout replay.

NVFP4 output directly from a GEMM.

In the π0.5\pi_{0.5} encoder feed-forward block, a GEMM produces two vectors, gate and up. The earlier path launched a separate kernel to compute GELU⁡(g​a​t​e)×u​p\operatorname{GELU}(gate)\mathbin{\times}up, quantize the result, and pack it for the next GEMM. FlashRT-PAI instead pairs gate and up weights when loading the checkpoint. That puts each pair of results next to each other inside the GEMM, allowing its epilogue to compute the product and write packed four-bit values and block scales directly in the next GEMM’s required layout. An initial fused version wrote a full-width result and doubled the next GEMM’s weight traffic, so its feed-forward chain was slower than the separate-kernel path. A compact, half-width store kept the next GEMM’s original shape; decision latency then fell, and the worst measured output cosine improved because the intermediate was quantized once rather than twice. The layout and producer–consumer format were designed and validated for this pipeline, not inferred from an ordinary operator graph.

A.4 Launch-Overlap Examples

Fetching weights before the activation is ready.

A GEMM cannot read an activation produced by the previous kernel until that kernel finishes, but its fixed weights are already available. FlashRT-PAI’s decoder GEMM starts streaming a few weight tiles before the wait, then loads the activation only after the dependency is satisfied. This shortened the decoder GEMM chain with identical outputs, but the gain was not monotonic: fetching all seven weight tiles early congested the memory queue, while two or three tiles worked best. Moving the release signal from the load warp to the multiply warp also gave up much of the benefit. The selected variant streams only the profitable prefix.

Choosing between persistent and separate GEMMs.

FlashRT-PAI also built a resident grid that runs several decoder GEMMs in one launch. Its load warp fetches the next GEMM’s weights while the current one finishes. With independent GEMMs, the chain ran faster than separate launches and came close to the measured memory-read ceiling. The version that also performs the required normalization between GEMMs, however, was slower than separate launches. The next GEMM must wait for the normalization result, and a grid-wide rendezvous adds cost that weight prefetch cannot hide. The implementation passed bit-exact checks but is disabled in the shipped path. A faster isolated chain was not a faster pipeline here; the useful rule is to fuse the memory-bound work between GEMMs, not every GEMM into one kernel.

Knowing when overlap has reached its limit.

More early work is not always better. In Thor tuning, extending early launch to RoPE, softmax, and FP8-conversion kernels produced no further measurable change. Prefetching the next layer’s weights into cache also slowed every tested variant of the decoder chain, because the prefetch competed with demand traffic. Together with the rejected persistent sequence above, these cases bound the technique: it can hide launch setup or input-independent memory traffic, but not work whose result the successor actually needs. FlashRT-PAI therefore tests overlap in the full pipeline as well as in isolated chains.

A.5 Execution-State Reuse Example

Instruction state.

The π0.5\pi_{0.5} action expert has ten denoising steps and eighteen layers; its adaptive-normalization values form a finite step-by-layer table for a given instruction. Rebuilding those values inside every decision repeats work whose input has not changed. FlashRT-PAI’s set_prompt builds the table and prompt embedding once, keeps them in named buffers, and lets later kernels select the needed row. A same-size prompt update overwrites the existing embedding rather than replacing its address; a device-side valid length masks padding without recapture. In an earlier compiler implementation, in-graph Dense GEMMs rebuilt these styles at every inference, and hand-editing that graph to precompute them reduced its latency. FlashRT-PAI uses the same temporal-hoisting idea in its prompt setup. The instruction lifetime and refresh rule specify when this prepared state can be reused and when it must be rebuilt.
